subject: Calculating log_lik in a model with two "stochastic" observables

messages.author: 900cd0718d2352a1
messages.subject: Calculating log_lik in a model with two "stochastic" observables
parts:
I'm a "Bayesian novice" and I'm trying to learn STAN by estimating a series of models on a dataset, and have a question regarding how I should construct the log_lik in the generated quantities block. 

The analysis assesses the association between daily smoking and suicides (based on a hypothesis from some epidemiological articles). Suicide data (and the size of the population in the different cells) are from administrative data and cover the entire Norwegian population. Data on daily smoking come from an annual series of representative surveys that can be grouped into the same age-sex categories.

Inspired by McElreath's book, I wanted to specify the model so that the sampling uncertainty from the survey is captured in the model. I assume that 
-daily smoker counts in any age-sex-year cell in the survey data are a binomial draw from a sample of known size with an underlying actual daily-smoking rate, and
-suicides in any age-sex-year cell are a poisson-distributed count from a lambda related to observable features of the cell (e.g., age, year, gender)
-there is residual variation in lambda across the cells due to unobserved differences, captured by a normally distributed term (alpha) that has a mean of 0.

My question: To calculate the log_lik for each observation, do I simply sum the log prob of the observed daily smoker counts and the log prob of the observed suicide counts? 

Using the most "complex" model as an example, my current attempt at doing this is the following generated quantities block (full model code attached):

generated quantities{
  vector[N_cells] y_rep;
  vector[N_cells] lambda;
  vector[N_cells] log_lik;
  
  for (n in 1:N_cells){
    lambda[n] = alpha[n]+sex_coef[sex[n]]+smoking_coef*smoking_rate_actual[n]+year_coef[period[n]]+age_coef[age_group[n]]+log(pop_count[n]);
    y_rep[n] = poisson_log_rng(lambda[n]);
    log_lik[n] = poisson_log_lpmf( suicide_count[n]| lambda[n] );
    log_lik[n] = log_lik[n]+ binomial_logit_lpmf(smoker_count[n]|sample_count[n],smoking_rate_actual[n]);

  }
}

Is this correct, or have I misunderstood something?

(FWIW - the most complex specification finds no association between smoking and suicides, while a model that does not account for the survey sampling uncertainty finds a substantial negative association - the opposite of the epidemiological hypothesis I set out to assess.)

Sincerely,

Ole Rogeberg

> My question: To calculate the log_lik for each observation, do I simply sum the log prob of the observed daily smoker counts and the log prob of the observed suicide counts?

I didn't quite follow what variables were observed from that description,
but the general point is that you need to marginalize out all the latent
data-dependent values, such as the true values in a measurement-error model
where you observe only the measured values. So the point is the likelihood
is just

p(observed | parameters) = INTEGRATE p(observed, latent | parameters) d.latent

or use a sum if the latent values are discrete. I think the latent here
is smoking_rate_actual and I don't know how to integrate it out. Others might.

- Bob
